trackText: The first Gemme is the moment when autumn shifts toward a wintry mood. In early November, the exhibition takes place at the very heart of the season: golden sunlight on the abbey walls, the kitchen roof standing out against a sky scattered with pink and orange clouds, leaves already red and yellow in the surrounding landscape. The body slips into a half-sleep.

The second Gemme is marked by intense humidity, the cool dampness I encountered repeatedly during my stay at the abbey. It could be titled “cold water”: the arrival of drizzle, cold showers broken by a few brief clear spells. The tuffeau stone walls tend to absorb the moisture easily, and the abbey takes on a deeper yellow hue.

The third Gemme celebrates days of strong wind. It involved placing the microphone high up, to hear how the leaves of different tree species shivered when confronted with gusts. Life also becomes much more inward.

The fourth Gemme speaks of growing darkness and the arrival of lights: the human appropriation of the night, preparations for the festivities, the illumination of the cloister, and the artworks scattered throughout the abbey. Nighttime hours become increasingly dominant, life is lived under artificial light. Celebration becomes a way to compensate.

The fifth Gemme reaches the solstice. It turns inward: the fireplace, warmth, and the crackling of flames. The hearth in its truest sense—anchors reinforced, thick walls, and the feeling of being sheltered from the cold.
